speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: the third reading of Bill No. C-110 to amend the Criminal Code.

Mr. Speaker, I have just a few remarks to make at the third reading stage of this bill. I should first like to recommend to the Minister of Justice, as well as other ministers who may be bringing legislation before this house, that an opportunity be given, particularly in regard to such serious matters as these, for more study prior to the introduction and passage of bills.
This bill was only placed before us at 11 o'clock yesterday morning and received second reading early last evening. It contains provisions of great import, and for the first time provides implementation of the McRuer commission's recommendations by the adoption of a definition and provisions dealing with those individuals now to be classed as dangerous sexual offenders. Because this is a matter which has been discussed for some period of time, there has been a body of opinion expressed already in regard to it. However, some of the other provisions which are included in the amendments contained in the bill have not had such careful study by any such persons.
These provisions are most important, although fortunately in Canada the segment of the population to which they apply is very small. The minister gave us the information that fewer than 40 people have been convicted under the prior provision respecting criminal sexual psychopaths. Nevertheless this problem affects 40 people, and for those and the public whom they may have irreparably damaged it is a serious matter and one which requires care and consideration.
The minister indicated that there are other parts of the report which still must necessarily be implemented. In particular he pointed out that research facilities called for by the commission have not yet been established. Unhappily those who will now be classed as dangerous sexual offenders are individuals who respond but little to any sort of training or treatment carried out by psychiatrists and people in the field. I suggest it is therefore necessary, Mr. Speaker, that research facilities be set up at once in order that modern science may have an opportunity to find a way to assist those people who are psychologically ill.
(Mr. Martin (Essex East).]
If clinics are to be instituted, then perhaps there should be not just one but a number of small ones. I note that in Le Devoir this morning there is a comment from a meeting of mental hygiene specialists in Vancouver with respect to the bill passed previously dealing with drug addicts. They are complaining that the government did not consult them before bringing in its provisions. In fact they suggest that a number of small clinics for the treatment of drug addicts is much preferable to one large one.
I suggest that the government consult those active in the field who have been studying the problem for some time before launching into a program. It is necessary immediately, now that the legislation has been passed, that the government engage personnel consisting of psychiatrists and other people for the training program, and that they commence a building program for research facilities and begin to allocate money and plans in order that those who may be convicted and incarcerated under preventive detention shall receive some assistance. Otherwise it is sterile to say that we will legislate only to segregate them from the population and forget about them after we have them behind bars.
In addition, there was a change in the legislation with respect to habitual criminals. We are fortunate in Canada in that since we have had this legislation only some 54 have been convicted as such and sent to prison. The same provisions are now to apply to those who are convicted on an application as habitual criminals, and they will be incarcerated for preventive detention. It is necessary as well that they receive psychiatric and psychological training and assistance in order that they may be restored to society. As is indicated by the figures, already there have been some habitual criminals restored as decent citizens, and it is apparent that they are good risks when they go back to the community.
The other important group of sections in the bill which has received second reading were those dealing with the small boats regulations. For the benefit of those who were not present may I say there was some discussion and a point was raised about the difficulty of policing. The regulations referred to are those which have already been in force under the responsibility of the Department of Transport. They are now moved into the Criminal Code. Neither the minister nor the members of this house should forget that the mere legislation is not enough. It is necessary to police it.
The hon. member for Kootenay West raised a most interesting point which found favour with the minister, namely that in order to assist provincial authorities in policing the

regulation it may be possible to call upon voluntary associations. The hon. member suggested that perhaps members of boating or yacht clubs would assist. The minister suggested it might be possible to do something along this line with respect to fire wardens or fish and game wardens. I urge upon the minister that this line be followed up because the legislation, without enforcement, is useless.
Briefly then, Mr. Speaker, may I say that the provisions are generally good ones, but they would have benefited from more study. More time should have elapsed between the presentation of the printed bill and the discussion in committee. I hope that before other amendments are brought forward more time will be allowed for study not only by the opposition but by members of the public interested in law enforcement and the code before adoption by this house.
Motion agreed to and bill read the third time and passed.

speechtext:
The house resumed from Monday, June 19, consideration of the motion of Mr. Hees for the second reading of Bill No. C-108, to amend the Export Credits Insurance Act.
Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Trade
and Commerce): Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to amend the Export Credits Insurance Act by increasing the resources available for the export financing facilities which I announced in the house last November. This financing makes it possible for Canadian exporters to sell capital equipment on long term credit to foreign buyers.
I should like to describe briefly the operations of the Export Credits Insurance Corporation, which is charged with the responsibility of administering the Export Credits Insurance Act. The corporation was originally established to insure Canadian exporters of goods and services against non-payment by foreign buyers. The corporation's annual report for 1960, which was tabled in the house on March 28, 1961 shows that in the 16 years of its insurance operations it insured for its own account and risk a total of $575 million of export sales. The excess of premiums over net losses and expenses is less than one fifth of 1 per cent of export sales insured. Thus as was intended, it has operated on what is practically a break-even basis.
In its insurance operations the Export Credits Insurance Corporation charges premiums related to the risks involved. Rates of premium are established by taking into
Export Credits Insurance Act account the commodity, the credit term, the buyer's country, the volume of the exporter's business, the spread of risk and any other considerations which in the view of the corporation affect the risks underwritten. The average rate of premium for all the short term business insured by the corporation to date is less than three quarters of 1 per cent. As a general rule the maximum credit term for short term business in 180 days. The insurance premium is a flat charge and not on a per annum basis.
Rates for medium term business, that is up to five years, also vary by country and credit term. While premiums for medium term business are also a flat rate charge they work out to about 1.5 per cent per annum on the amount at risk. It should be emphasized that the corporation is not trying to make a profit. On the other hand, neither does it subsidize export sales. The premiums which it charges will in the long run, it is hoped, result in a break-even operation. The maximum liability the corporation may take on for its own account is $200 million. This is under section 14 of the act.
In cases where the board of directors of the corporation is of the opinion that a proposed contract of insurance would impose upon the corporation a liability for a term or an amount in excess of that which the corporation would normally undertake, and if in the opinion of the Minister of Trade and Commerce it is in the national interest that the proposed contract of insurance be entered into, the governor in council may authorize the corporation to issue the insurance policy. In such cases any loss would be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund. Under this section of the act the corporation has insured a total of $360 million of export sales, and there have been no claims.
With the backing of export credits insurance an exporter has no difficulty in getting short term financing from the chartered banks. Even in times when domestic credit has been tight, the Canadian chartered banks have been willing and able to finance short term export business.
To take care of medium term export financing the nine Canadian chartered banks have together established the Export Finance Corporation of Canada, Limited. The Export Finance Corporation has an authorized capital of $50 million, and with this as a base could borrow up to $500 million to finance exports from Canada on medium term credit. This Export Finance Corporation, which recently commenced operations with Mr. H. Duke Scott as general manager, has announced it will finance capital goods transactions involving credit up to five years where the sales are

Export Credits Insurance Act backed by export credits insurance. This is a first class example ol co-operation between government and business for the benefit of the Canadian economy as a whole.
Under section 21A of the act the corporation may, when authorized by the governor in council, guarantee the obligations of a foreign buyer and may also purchase or sell the guaranteed obligations and lend money upon the security of guaranteed instruments. It is by using this authority that the government has undertaken to finance export sales of capital goods for periods extending beyond five years at rates of interest approximately equal to those being offered by major competitors. Government financing is, however, available only for capital goods having a high Canadian content-80 per cent or better-and which are intended for use in economically sound projects in creditworthy countries where it is reasonable to expect continuing foreign sales.
The normal procedure would be that the Export Credits Insurance Corporation would guarantee, by endorsement or otherwise, the long term obligations given by a foreign buyer to a Canadian exporter. The corporation would then "purchase" the obligations, thus giving the exporter cash. The exporter gets cash on the barrel head and the foreign buyer in effect gets a long term credit. If a particular lender were interested in holding the obligations for the interest return the corporation could then "sell" the guaranteed obligations to that lender.
The present intention is that the interest rate charged for a long term loan for export financing would be about 1 per cent above the cost to the government of borrowing money. Thus the rate quoted today is in the order of 6 per cent. This rate makes us competitive with other long term lenders such as the export-import bank of Washington.
There is no fixed or statutory limitation to the period of credit which might be approved. The factors that would be taken into account would be the size or value of the project involved; the useful life or operating period of the equipment; the ability of the buying country to pay, and the terms of payment that would be granted by international lenders such as the world bank or by the export-import bank.

speechtext:
Section 21B of the act provides that the limitation of liability for both insurance under section 21 and financing under section 21A is $200 million. As at May 31, 1961 insurance in force under section 21 totals $138 million and financing commitments under section 21A total $48 million, making $186 million in all. This leaves only $14 million available for both additional insurance under section 21 and any long term financing under section 21 A. As stated in the explanatory note to the bill:
The purpose of this bill is to provide that the two hundred million dollar limit of liability specified in section 21B of the act, now applicable to both contracts of insurance entered into by the corporation under section 21 and instruments guaranteed by the corporation under section 21A, be made applicable solely to contracts of insurance entered into under section 21. The bill would also provide a separate limit, in the amount of two hundred million dollars, on the liability of importers under outstanding instruments guaranteed by the corporation under section 21A.
Since the government announced the availability of financing for sales of capital goods on long term credit, applications totalling about $250 million have been received. This is a good indication of the potential export volume of capital goods business. A number of projects have been approved by the committee on export finance, and commitments totalling $48 million have been given. Of the remainder, those which are considered to be eligible for financing are under active examination at this moment.
As I stated in my remarks when presenting the resolution in connection with this proposed amendment to the Export Credits Insurance Act, I am delighted to have to ask parliament to increase the funds available for long term financing. This is another example of the steps which this government is taking to encourage Canadian manufacturers and exporters to enter into the export markets of the world and increase their export sales. Backed by export credit insurance and export credit financing, it is up to the exporters to get out and seek orders from buyers who will buy if delivery is prompt, quality and design are good, and the price is right.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LIMITS OF LIABILITY UNDER SECTION 21
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the minister for his statement. I regret the last sentence or two of it because of a slight historical inaccuracy. It is an inaccuracy that is not too important, and it does not in any way detract from the importance of the legislation and the desirability of the bill. The inaccuracy was quite simple and it was this. The necessity for this bill is due to the failure of the government to listen to question raised by hon. members of the opposition in 1959

when section 21A was added to the bill. What we are doing today is correcting that situation.
However, the amendment is none the less desirable. It is better to be late than never to correct these little omissions, and this was an important omission. I merely wish to correct the minister, because I should not like him to be misled as to what this legislation is, and I should not wish his actions as minister heading up this extremely important department to be influenced by a wrong concept on his part as to the legislation.
The minister is quite right in stressing the importance of this legislation and of the new amendment in relation to the possible export of capital goods. I have always regarded this as a particularly fortunate piece of legislation in the Canadian economy. We have the fact that action was taken one year before the end of the war to bring in this legislation in order to meet what then was the problem in the export market, namely making it possible for our former regular customers to buy our goods through the provisions of the act. Amendments to this act year after year through the intervening 17 years since it was first brought into operation have I think kept the act in a healthy condition and rendered it very useful to our export trade.
The first act was passed in 1944 and was dealt with by the then minister of trade and commerce, the late Hon. J. A. MacKinnon. The first act provided for insurance against the risk of loss arising out of non-payment. As hon. members will recall, it was then basically a matter of payment and exchange control and the uncertainty of exchange all over the world. That act performed its functions. Then in 1945 the then minister of finance introduced a bill amending part of the act to provide for the lending to other government's former customers, of certain sums of money which were very large in relation to the finances as viewed in those days, though perhaps not so large in relation to the figures we hear from finance ministers these days in the House of Commons. However, they were very large then.
Although I have not the reference, I recall many times hearing the hon. member for Greenwood speak about this legislation and some of the benefits that flowed from it. It was interesting that in 1945 two hon. members in the house were rather concerned about what was then this very new legislation because is was advancing and increasing foreign trade and we might forget our home market. It was rather interesting to find that view was asserted by the then hon. member for Davenport, the late Mr. MacNicol. It also seemed to be supported by the hon. member
Export Credits Insurance Act for Rosedale of that day; I refer to Mr. Jackman. I am sure that Mr. Jackman would be the first to agree now that the bill has worked well and that his fears were not in any way justified.
Then in 1948 the bill was again amended in order to meet the changing situation, and the area of insurance was enlarged. Provisions were introduced which enabled the corporation to meet the situation where the liability was in an amount in excess of that which the corporation would normally undertake in relation to any one contract, export, commodity or country. I have references to the hon. member for Greenwood who took an interest in that bill at that time; and I must say that, to his credit, he raised the question of why private insurers were not in this field. It was clear that they were not in it, and I think the need for this legislation has been demonstrated since then.
Then in 1954 there were further amendments to the act. The amendments in 1954 were to increase the capital. The amount of insurance permitted under the ordinary insurance provisions is 10 times the amount of subscribed capital and the amount of the reserve. The capital provision was increased, but in effect the amount of insurance permitted was increased from $100 million to $200 million under the ordinary provisions. That is section 13 of the act.
Incidentally, I may say that at the committee stage I wish to raise a very small point having to do with reserves. The act itself refers to reserves in the financial accounts; two items of reserve are used. What is referred to is the one item only of the reserve, or that is what was intended to be referred to in determining the amount of insurance that could be granted. However, that is a small matter of not too great importance and can be referred to at the committee stage.
Then in 1957 the former government again amended the act and enlarged its scope in relation to the type of goods that could be shipped, and the purposes; that is to say goods for consignment, goods for exhibition and so on. Later in the same year, namely in 1957, after the change of government the new minister of trade and commerce again submitted an amendment increasing the amount of insurance that could be undertaken under the contracts of insurance which the corporation was empowered to enter into under section 21 of the act. That was the section having to do with those types of contracts that the corporation normally would not undertake but which could be undertaken with the approval of the governor in council when certain criteria were met. The former

Export Credits Insurance Act minister of trade and commerce increased the limitation under that section from $100 to $200 million.
Then, again in 1959, the former minister introduced the amendments which provided the right of the corporation to discount paper, to guarantee paper, and it is that 1959 provision that is being amended by the bill before us. That was to meet the new demand in the export markets having to do with financing.
It is interesting to observe the change in the problems of the export trade over the years. Formerly it was a question of the countries to which they were selling being able to obtain exchange with which to pay for the goods. Then it was the other risks related to that point. Then it was the question of enlarging the type of insurance we could grant because of the size of some contracts, notably some of the wheat contracts and related matters. In these cases there were risks that because of their size would be so great that a prudent insurance company would not undertake them in relation to one customer.
Then in the last two years we have had the problem that is relatively new but very, very important. This is the problem of the difficulty of exporters financing their sales contracts and their paper. In any event, as far as I am concerned I hope that whatever governments are in office over the years, particular care will be paid to this legislation to see that it is adapted from year to year to meet the problems of exporters, in the way it has been over the past 17 years. I have no doubt at all in my own mind but that this legislation, in that very difficult conversion period after the war, was of very great assistance in getting our exporters into the markets of the world. I have no doubt at all that this kind of assistance will be required in the trading world of tomorrow to meet the very tough type of competition we will have to meet.
The minister said something this morning with relation to the activities of a privately owned corporation which was incorporated, incidentally, in 1959 if I remember correctly, to enter this field of guaranteeing and discounting export paper. It is somewhat unfortunate that the name of that corporation is remarkably similar to the name of this crown-owned corporation, but since there is a relatively small number of persons dealing with the two corporations perhaps there is not too much difficulty caused by that fact. It would have been a matter of real concern were the corporations of such a nature that a great many persons in the country dealt with them. I hope that the House of Commons will in the future take more care in


the granting of names to corporations than it has in the past, because I feel we have been a little careless on this subject over the years, and certainly we have a good example of this in the legislature before us at the moment.
I was not able to hear part of the minister's remarks this morning on the subject of the activities of the private corporation in this field, but I take it I can deal with that subject more closely in the committee stage and perhaps ask the minister to repeat part of his remarks at that time. I take it that the main concern now is for this public corporation to supplement the activities of the private corporation and deal with those types of contracts that cannot receive assistance through the private corporation.
There is one other matter I should like to mention. During the opening part of his remarks on second reading last evening the minister made reference to the contracts of insurance covering the sale of wheat to Poland. Indeed, this legislation has been used as the vehicle for insuring types of sales like the wheat sale to Poland and in former years to Czechoslovakia, I think, and Russia. There may be one or two others. The point I want to make now is this. The very large wheat sale to China apparently does not come under this legislation at all, and the insurance of the payment under those contracts of sale is dealt with separately by the government.
I would hope the government would not develop the practice of only providing part of the insurance and financing provisions that are properly granted to exporters from time to time. I would hope we would not develop a system of having parts of these contracts insured by the government under some other general authority or some other act, and sidetracking this act. As a matter of fact I have always regretted that the sale of wheat was taken away from the Minister of Trade and Commerce and put under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Agriculture. If I recall correctly, I referred to the somewhat truncated functions of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. It seemed to me that so many of the functions that were properly those of the Minister of Trade and Commerce had been taken away from him. In my opinion it was not a satisfactory way in which these matters should be dealt with. In any event, it is not for me to plead the cause of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, but this does pose real problems in the control parliament is to have over expenditures and risks of this sort. It does seem to me to weaken the efficiency of cabinet handling of the responsibilities in this field of export trade. I would hope that the minister responsible for export trade would be left with that responsibility and

fixed with it so that he is answerable for it.
The wheat sale to China is a very important transaction, and in relation to that sale we have no method of obtaining the proper information in the House of Commons. There is no requirement that the related contracts having to do with the insurance and guarantees of payment be tabled, as there is under this legislation. There is no way of getting the information that is ordinarily very important under these types of export contracts for other goods.
For instance, that contract provides for payment in foreign currency. So far as I recall this is the first contract in which we have accepted foreign currency in payment. That is the sort of thing that should be dealt with and examined by the Minister of Trade and Commerce because of the implications that impinge directly on our foreign trade. Whether it is a good thing to do, or is necessary, is another matter. The point is that it is the Minister of Trade and Commerce who should be examining the consequences, in relation to our exports and imports, of taking payments in foreign currency and assessing them.
There is the question of the information which is made available to the house. We have a very elaborate procedure set out in this legislation to guarantee that the house shall have full information; the annual report, the tabling of documents, and so on. If the government takes certain export insurance out of the ambit of this act, as was done in the case of the China wheat agreement, we have no information available to us. I asked a simple question when the minister gave the volume of the Chinese wheat contract sale. I asked him what rate of exchange he had used in computing the figures, because that makes a great difference as all hon. members will realize. I was not given that information, though it is information which is relevant.

There is another point which arises. Under this export credits insurance legislation, orders in council are required to be tabled and as a result we are able to examine the payments made and ascertain any default in payments. Indeed, some orders in council were tabled on June 9 dealing with that very point. There is one in relation to heavy equipment from the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation. I must say that in 1959 when the provision was first introduced I expected it would be used to a considerable extent. However, I think I am correct in saying that in the first year after the passing of the section there was no paper guaranteed or discounted under that section and that up to date it has amounted to a very small item. I believe there is now considerable activity, though, and it may become of real significance. As I say, I expected in 1959 that it would have been used a great deal right away. Apparently it was not, and if the minister has any explanation to give I should be interested to hear it.

This is not a matter which interests us now; it has more or less been shoved under the rug, but I am just as convinced as I am that I stand here now that the time will come when hon. members of this house will realize that this is one of the most important questions which will face us.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister whether it would be possible under this legislation to insure contracts which may be made under the arrangement with the Chinese government at Peking, providing the government decided to use this act? Is this act available for that purpose?

Mr. Chairman, I am advised that there is no reason why this legislation could not be used for that purpose. Of course the reason it was impossible to do so, as I explained in my opening remarks, is that there is available at the present time, until this measure is passed, as I hope it will be, only $14 million for use. The Chinese deal would have required much more than that.

Mr. Chairman, in respect to subsequent contracts which may be signed, based on this agreement with the government in Peking, this legislation, as the minister has said, could be used for insurance purposes. I take it if that were done then
any orders in council dealing with the matter of insurance on contracts to the government at Peking would be made public?
If this legislation is used for insuring future deals the orders in council will then be made public, yes.

Mr. Chairman, as I understand the Chinese wheat agreement it includes the requirement of keeping available the amount of wheat required over the term required, and that there are specific contracts dealing with precise numbers of bushels to be shipped within precise periods. As I recall the very limited information given in regard to this matter there is only one of the small contracts signed to date, and it would be the payment under these small contracts that would be insured. If I am correct in that recollection, it is then open to the authorities to have the payments on these small contracts insured under this act. Is it the intention of the government to do that?

Export Credits Insurance Act

Mr. Chairman, as the hon. member will realize, sales of wheat to China do not come under my department but under the Department of Agriculture. As to what will be the policy of handling future deals, this is something that the government as a whole will decide.
There are two answers to that. I must remind the minister that he is still a member of the government, at least that is the last intimation we have had.
I said the government as a whole.

We do have collective responsibility for the ministers, I think. As far as the committee is concerned the minister must answer for the government. But there is also another point. He is the minister responsible for administering this act. In his capacity as the minister responsible for administering this act I would like him to get information for the committee on whether the contracts dealing with specific shipments of wheat to China will be insured or dealt with under this legislation.

I must remind the hon. member that the outstanding wheat deals with China were not carried out by my department but by the wheat board, which now comes under the Department of Agriculture. As to how any future deals will be handled, this is something for the government as a whole to decide. I am afraid I cannot advise the committee how such future deals will be handled.

I must point out to the minister the arrangement for dealing with this sale of wheat to China. There was what was called a contract by the Minister of Agriculture dealing with the requirement to make available a certain number of bushels, and certain general things of that sort. It was alleged by other hon. members in the house that that was not a contract. Whether it was or not I was never able to find out because it just has not been before the house, and there is no way of finding out. In any event, it did become quite clear that whatever the arrangement was, provisions as to the amount to be shipped and the price to be paid for it came under the smaller contracts that were to be dealt with from time to time; I think the time indicated by the minister was every five months.
My question is addressed to those smaller, specific contracts that have to do with the payment and the quantities. Of course it is at that point that the insurance arises, but surely the government must have taken a decision on the methods of insuring or dealing with the risk involved in a sale of this magnitude, and that must be a decision on


government records by now. I ask the minister to get this information, because the committee is entitled to it and it is strictly relevant to the item now before us. I do not see any method by which the minister, with all his genial good nature, can escape that responsibility. It is a simple, direct responsibility, and it is a simple direct request from a member of the committee. It is proper information and it will be welcomed.

I acknowledge it is a simple, direct question, but I am afraid I am not in a position to answer it because all the details of the China wheat deal were handled by my colleague the Minister of Agriculture under whom the wheat board operates. I suggest to the hon. member that he satisfy his curiosity -a very understandable curiosity-about those deals by asking the Minister of Agriculture under whom they were carried out. They were not carried out by me or by my department, and I am afraid I am not in a position to answer the questions the hon. member has put to me.

I am very sorry. I can accept the minister's statement that he is not able to give us this information, but the situation is that I want to satisfy my curiosity about how this deal before us is to be administered before I can pass judgment on the propriety of the clause now before the committee. It is that curiosity that must be satisfied, and it must be satisfied by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Therefore I can only suggest to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that he obtain from the government the decision that is relevant to this particular legislation and advise the committee what it was. The other details of the wheat agreement, of course, I am not able to obtain at this time, or under this legislation, but this information I am entitled to obtain.

The excerpt which the minister read from the booklet put out by the Export Credits Insurance Corporation deals with the provisions of section 21A of the act. We are now dealing with clause 1 which amends section 21, which is the insurance provision of the act. This is the clause under which all the wheat sales are insured. I could give the reference to some of the wheat sales, if it is desired, which are insured under section 21, which is the clause now before the committee. I do not think that is necessary. But if the minister will refer to order in council P.C. 1961/311, which was tabled on June 9, 1961, he will find that that insures the sale to Czechoslovakia of 200,000 tons of wheat valued at approximately $17 million. The excerpts the minister read from the booklet of the corporation have reference to the financing operations on capital goods which are governed by clause 2 of the bill before us and which have not yet been reached by the committee.

I can give the hon. member for Ottawa West the information he is asking for. Since the act first came into operation there have been total wheat sales of $188,446,819 insured. If he wishes I can give him a breakdown of the countries.
I do not require that.
These are the sales that have been insured since the coming into operation of the act and up to the present day. The sales to China have not yet been insured under this act.
Will this legislation cover insurance of sales contracts for which payment is to be received by the Canadian exporter in a currency other than Canadian dollars?
Yes, Mr. Chairman. We will insure in any convertible currency. Usually it is in Canadian dollars, United States dollars or sterling, but we will insure in any convertible currency.

What efforts are being made to let exporters in the Atlantic and western

Export Credits Insurance Act provinces know of the availability of the benefits of this legislation? The minister mentioned that 268 companies had taken advantage of the legislation. Almost all of them are located in either Quebec or Ontario. Is a sufficient effort being made to let the exporters in the Atlantic and western provinces, and British Columbia in particular, know of the availability of the benefits?

I am very glad to be able to answer that question. In order that businessmen in every part of the country should be made familiar with the services which the Department of Trade and Commerce puts at their disposal, we have already held trade and industrial promotion conferences in four of the provinces, three of them in western Canada-British Columbia, Alberta and Manitoba-and one in eastern Canada, in Ontario.
I have advised all the provincial governments that my department is not only willing but is very anxious to go to any province that requests us to do so and to hold one of these trade promotion conferences. A representative of the Export Credits Insurance Corporation is present at each conference. He outlines specifically to the businessmen what services are available through the Export Credits Insurance Corporation both with regard to insuring the sale of goods and with regard to making long term capital available. The representative is there not only to outline what we can do but to answer all questions.
I might say that at all these conferences a great many questions have been directed to the representative of the corporation, the president or the vice president, and a great deal of interest has been shown by the businessmen who have attended. We hope that every province will invite us to hold a conference in the latter part of the year, because we feel the information we are able to give and the information we are able to gain from the businessmen attending is very considerable. I can assure the hon. member that the conference held in Vancouver, where we met the businessmen of his own province of British Columbia, was very well attended and a great deal of interest was shown in the facilities made available by the Export Credits Insurance Corporation.

Have any conferences been held in the Atlantic provinces? Are any planned there? It would seem to me that area would perhaps find this type of assistance more beneficial than any other part of Canada.

Export Credits Insurance Act in the other Atlantic provinces as well. I agree with the hon. member that this kind of information would be most useful to businessmen in the Atlantic provinces, and we are very eager to give it.

That is right.

Export Credits Insurance Act exports. I am wondering whether the application of this $2 million limitation would be so stringent as to restrict a proposition of that kind.

We have had no requests, I am advised, for long term financing, which is in access of five years, for amounts less than $2 million, to answer the hon. member's question. I should like to ask the minister whether other commonwealth countries are contemplated in respect of assistance under this special provision. I am thinking particularly of those nations in Africa which are now commonwealth members or dependencies, which are so dependent upon agriculture and are carrying on this agriculture under very primitive conditions. What is new about it is that the technique of calling insuring under this act "aid" is a new use of the language. That is really what bothers a great many people. That is the new thing that has been done that is apparently causing confusion. I thought all hon. members in the house had spotted that when the announcement was made.

I have not at any time referred to insurance as aid or short term financing as aid.

On clause 2-Definitions.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO RATES ON RAPESEED
speechtext:
The purpose of this bill is to apply to rapeseed the railway freight rates applicable to flaxseed under the Crowsnest pass agreement. At the present time subsections 6 and 7 of section 328 of the Railway Act read as follows:
(6)	Notwithstanding anything in subsection (5). rates on grain and flour shall, on and from the twenty-seventh day of June, 1925, be governed by the provisions of the agreement made pursuant to chapter 5 of the statutes of Canada 1897, but such rates shall apply to all such traffic moving from all points on all lines of railway west of Fort William to Fort William or Port Arthur over all lines now or hereafter constructed by any company subject to the jurisdiction of parliament.
(7)	The board shall not excuse any charge of unjust discrimination, whether practised against shippers, consignees, or localities or of undue or unreasonable preference respecting rates on grain and flour governed by the provisions of chapter 5 of the statutes of Canada 1897 and by the agreement made or entered into pursuant thereto within the territory referred to in subsection (6) on the ground that such discrimination or preference is justified or required by the said act or by the agreement made or entered into pursuant thereto.
Those two subsections set out the principles of the Crowsnest pass freight rate legislation. As the house knows, these rates have been in existence since 1897. At that time rapeseed was not listed, and it was not considered a grain because it was practically unknown, or at any rate it was not grown on the prairies. However, at the present time rapeseed is an important oilseed grain in western Canada. If hon. members would look at the figures they will see that they are very impressive. In 1960, 550,000 acres were seeded to this crop in Saskatchewan, 170,000 acres in Alberta and 36,000 acres in Manitoba.
Under the provisions of subsections 6 and 7 of section 328 of the Railway Act the rates on grain and flour from points west of Fort William and Port Arthur to those ports and
Railway Act
to the Pacific coast are required to be governed by the provisions of the Crowsnest pass agreement.
Rapeseed is recognized as a grain within the accepted definition of that term and is classified as a grain under the Canada Grain Act. It has not, however, been recognized as a grain for the purpose of freight rates pursuant to the Crowsnest pass agreement.
On June 10, 1960 the board of transport commissioners rejected an application to have rapeseed classified as a grain under the Crowsnest pass agreement, but the board did not question that rapeseed was, in fact, a grain. Its ruling was based on the fact that rape-seed was not grown as a grain in western Canada at the time the Crowsnest pass agreement was reached. The purpose of the present bill is not to place rapeseed within the terms of the Crowsnest pass agreement but to apply to rapeseed the same rates as are applicable to flaxseed under the Crownest pass agreement.
The amendment provided by the present bill will add a new subsection 8 to section 328 of the Railway Act to provide that the reference to "grain" in subsections 6 and 7 shall include rapeseed, and that the rates applicable to rapeseed shall not exceed those applicable to flaxseed.
I think the effect of this legislation will be to make the growing of rapeseed more attractive to the farmers of western Canada and provide them with the possibility of an interesting return for the rapeseed grown. The great advantage of this will be that rapeseed will take the place, to a greater extent, of other cereals grown on the prairies, and this will have a tendency to reduce the acreage of cereal grains whose disposal is now presenting a considerable problem. The provision and consumption of domestic oil and meal should also assist the Canadian economy in a general way by reducing the volume of imports from other countries. Another effect of this reduction of freight rates on rapeseed will be, I think, to make it possible for this cereal to be sold as animal feed at a price attractive enough to realize a good market for this product.
As a member coming from the province of Quebec I think I have extended my knowledge of the grain situation on the prairies, and I hope my friends from that region have not detected too many bad errors in what I have said. I know the whole situation will be extremely well explained by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale (Mr. Rapp), who has been carrying on a tremendous campaign for the recognition of the importance of this grain ever since he has been in this house. I know this conscientious member will discuss this matter at some length, and

Railway Act
I should like to take the opportunity of congratulating him for his continuous backing of this important legislation. I think the farmers of Canada as a whole should be very proud in knowing that an hon. member who is wholeheartedly in support of a piece of legislation such as this can, by continuous effort, sell his idea to his colleagues in the house and accomplish the passage of that legislation, thereby rendering great service to the country and to his farmer friends on the prairie.
Mr. Speaker, I should also like to point out that later I will have one of my colleagues move an amendment to this bill adding the date upon which this legislation will come into effect. The intention of that amendment is to see that this measure will come into force on the 1st day of August, 1961, which is the beginning of the new crop year. This will give to our farmers in western Canada the opportunity of taking advantage of this piece of legislation.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO RATES ON RAPESEED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are pleased that the government has seen fit to introduce this bill, but we think it is long overdue. We feel the result it will have will be equality of treatment, as far as freight rates are concerned, to the producers of rapeseed.
This subject is not new in this house but has been discussed by members of parliament on many occasions in recent years. The former member for Humboldt-Melfort, Mr. Alexander Bryson, pioneered in this field, as hon. members who were here at that time I am sure will recall. I remember that very often when Mr. Bryson raised questions in regard to rape in this house many hon. members snickered because they were not certain just what he was referring to. However, the question of rape or rapeseed has been raised in this house on many occasions, along with requests that freight rates be applied to rape-seed in the same manner as applied to other grain under the Crowsnest pass agreement.
The bill now before the house has been brought in following requisitions made by farm organizations of this country which have recognized the present injustice as well as the growing importance of rapeseed within the agriculture industry. I should also like to say that on many occasions the present member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale-perhaps one day this riding will also include the

name of Wadena-has presented a good case for this kind of adjustment in the freight rate regarding rapeseed, and we are pleased at this time that the bill is being given support by all sides of the house. I also want to congratulate the minister on his wide knowledge of this subject and on the informative manner in which he handled the introduction of this bill, and particularly on his comprehensive answer to the question posed by the hon. member for Kootenay West.
During this session the minister has been extending his knowledge into many fields and we appreciate the comprehensiveness of his remarks when he pointed out so well that while this will be of particular benefit to the producers of western Canada, none the less it will be of national benefit as well. It will be a potential benefit to livestock feeders outside the prairie provinces. While it is a small contribution to the over-all problem, it should at least in a minor way reduce our great dependence on imports of commodities from the United States. Therefore on all counts it is a measure which should commend itself to the house at this time.
It is particularly gratifying to me, Mr. Speaker, since it runs against the propaganda directed against the Crowsnest rates in recent years. The enemies of the Crowsnest rates have been attempting to destroy them. Far from being successful, we have an indication today that parliament is going to reaffirm those rates by providing their necessary and justifiable extension to rapeseed. With the passage of this legislation not only the rapeseed producers but western producers generally will take satisfaction from the fact that parliament is reaffirming and strengthening the argument in favour of the Crowsnest rates.
I do not think it would be appropriate for me to have the complete text of my remarks consist of approbation and compliments. I think I should make some constructive suggestions to the minister. The question of rapeseed is very important in many parts of western Canada, including the constituency of the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale. Maybe he could get those three communities to agree to use just the initials from now on; if we could do so we might shorten the duration of the session. This, of course, could apply to the names of a great many constituencies in the house.
Rapeseed is important in the hon. member's riding and in a great many other constituencies. In the important and well known constituency of Assiniboia, where there are producers as efficient as producers in other ridings, we are getting into the production of another grain that in the days ahead may have a real economic importance. I refer to
Railway Act
the production of mustard seed. A great many farmers in that particular part of Saskatchewan sowed mustard this spring on a contract basis. Therefore it would be most appropriate if the minister would give the same kind of sympathetic consideration toward extending the rates to mustard seed that apply to rapeseed. I should think it would get the general approval of the house in the same way this bill is getting the approval of hon. members.
Western farmers have been advised to diversify their crops. They have never been short of advice, and they have never minded taking it so long as they could see some economic advantage in accepting it. The production of rapeseed will undoubtedly have increasing importance in the years ahead. I suggest that to further stimulate the diversification of crops on the prairies and to bring about equality of treatment in the freight rates applying to the various grains the minister should give consideration to the suggestion I make, so that the producers of mustard seed in my part of Canada will have the same well deserved advantages under the Crowsnest pass rates now to be enjoyed by the producers of rapeseed.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO RATES ON RAPESEED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted, and it gives me a great deal of pleasure, to support the proposed amendment to the Railway Act to apply to rapeseed the rates applicable to flaxseed by virtue of the Crowsnest pass agreement.
My first words should be to congratulate the Minister of Transport on bringing in this timely and very important bill so far as the western grain producers are concerned. I would also be remiss in my duties were I not anxious to give credit to those who have played such an important role in this historic event for our agricultural industry. I know only too well that had it not been for the keen interest of our Prime Minister in the welfare of agriculture and in particular his keen interest in the rapeseed producers, this legislation would never have come in. If it had not been for the hard working Minister of Agriculture, who has done everything possible to put agriculture on a sound economic basis, and if it had not been for the sympathetic understanding of the cabinet, this historic event would never have occurred.
Much credit must also go to my good friend the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin). This learned gentleman, together with the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Wool-liams), so ably presented the rapeseed case before the board of transport commissioners it is my belief that this actually laid the foundation for having rapeseed classified by

Railway Act
the board of transport commissioners as a grain. The decision of the board was unanimous. All these contributions were really important and instrumental in bringing in this bill. I would be remiss if I did not mention also the members from the three western provinces who appeared before the board of transport commissioners as witnesses and were anxious to take the witness stand and give evidence to the effect that rapeseed is a grain.
This is the day for which the rapeseed producers have been waiting for 18 years. This is the day when justice has been rendered after a long and relentless struggle by the western farmers to bring rapeseed under the Crowsnest pass agreement. This is the day when the name of John G. Diefenbaker will be inscribed in the hearts of the western farmers. Whatever else will be said, credit must go to the Prime Minister and the members of the treasury benches because they were the ones who brought about this legislation.
Let me also say, Mr. Speaker, that I would be less than fair were I not also to give credit to the opposition. Ever since I have had the opportunity of speaking in this house as a member of parliament on behalf of the rapeseed producers, of whom I have many in my constituency, the opposition have always supported me wholeheartedly in my presentations and have given me much appreciated assistance. They never disappointed me in this respect.
It would appear as though I knew this in advance, because if one refers to my maiden speech in this house on May 26, 1958 one finds that I expressed the following opinion of the opposition. Let me quote what I said at that time. After congratulating the Prime Minister on his overwhelming victory I said as recorded on page 477 of Hansard:
My heartiest congratulations go also to the ministers of the cabinet, to members of our party both senior and junior, and to all hon. members of either parties, too, who are here to serve Canada in whatever capacity they may be called upon to do so. We who are conscious of the merits of our democratic system will appreciate very much their constructive contributions so that we can all serve the Canadian people in this parliament to the best of our ability.
It has been very gratifying to me to find that the opposition has not disappointed me in this respect. I know my rapeseed producers in the west would want me to say these things about our cabinet, our Prime Minister and our opposition.
Before I deal with the bill itself I should like to let you, Mr. Speaker, into a well concealed secret. It concerns a person by the name of Mr. Rapeseed, who is a good friend of mine of long standing. He was born and

raised in the west. I could almost say that we grew up together in the prairie provinces. My friendship with Mr. Rapeseed is a long and intimate one. When I was elected to this house in 1958 Mr. Rapeseed told me that he was going to come down to Ottawa and sit beside me in the House of Commons. Of course I told him this was impossible; after all, only elected members are allowed to be in the House of Commons. However, he insisted and he assured me that he would remain invisible, thus doing me no harm.
After following me to Ottawa he followed me in the corridors and every place I went, constantly whispering in my ear "Don't forget to mention Mr. Rapeseed". He would come and sit beside me in the house. Every time I rose to speak he would whisper in my ear "Don't forget to mention Mr. Rapeseed". Being a good friend of mine, I had no alternative but to follow his advice. He even followed me into the caucus. Of course, Mr. Speaker, you do not expect that I would reveal anything that occurred in that holy place, except to say that he was very bold and he was very insistent that I mention his name continually. He was with me when I visited the ministers' offices. He would not miss, for anything, my visits to the Prime Minister. He really enjoyed those. He always sat beside me and said "Don't forget to mention Mr. Rapeseed".
On the last of such visits he insisted that I take a picture of the Prime Minister, myself and Mr. Rapeseed. Again, because he was a good friend of mine, I did take a picture. He was bold enough, too, to insist that I take a picture of the Minister of Agriculture, who he said was a very good friend of his of long standing. This picture turned out not too badly. Once he conceived the idea that a picture would serve him well and help him advertise his name, he became so bold as to suggest that pictures of Mr. Rapeseed and myself should be sent to every member of parliament, every member of the Senate and the members of the press gallery. If anyone wants to see a picture of Mr. Rapeseed, together with his biography, I shall be very pleased to show them. I received many replies to this document from the members of the other place, even from Mr. Speaker, who was very pleased to meet Mr. Rapeseed.
But something happened here today. When I came down to the House of Commons he stopped me again and said, "Mr. Rapp, I am very sorry but this is going to be my last trip to the house. I am a native of the prairie provinces, and I must go back to the place where I belong." Then he said, "Of course, times have changed now; I can travel much cheaper on the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific railways. I shall take advantage of that and go back to my own province."

He asked me what I would like him to say when he gets back to the prairie provinces. I told him that he should help the Canadian grain producers to reduce their acreages of wheat and be a good friend. This is the story of Mr. Rapeseed.
Now, speaking to the bill itself, I find that I have a good deal of material prepared on the subject of rapeseed. In looking over my files and in looking over the many speeches I have made here on the subject, I discovered that there is not one thing I have not said about rapeseed. Since there are so many of my good friends from Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, and I am sure some members of the opposition, who would like the opportunity to speak on this subject today, I thought it would be a waste of time to give you some of my old, warmed over speeches on rapeseed to which you have listened during the last three and a half years. I thought I should give other hon. members the opportunity to tell you the story of rapeseed. They are just as interested in the subject as I am, although in my constituency, as the hon. member for Assiniboia said, more rapeseed is grown than in any other place in western Canada.
I know that rapeseed has a great future. It will serve our purpose well, that is to take acreage out of wheat production. Mr. Speaker, as a western farmer and a member representing one of the rapeseed growing areas of Manitoba, it gives me a lot of pleasure to support the action of this government in introducing Bill No. C-lll, to amend the Railway Act designating rapeseed as a grain under the terms of the Railway Act. The fact that this important oilseed crop will enjoy the same freight rate as that now prevailing for flax will not only make it a more profitable alternative for wheat but will place farmers in a better competitive position in the export market.

I think this afternoon shows that most all hon. members are aware-and I think the producers of this crop should know-that it was largely through the persistent efforts of one of our western colleagues that the proposed amendment was brought before parliament. The logic of the argument used by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tis-dale, not only as a witness before the board of transport commissioners but in pleading his case in this house, left no doubt in the mind of anyone that he was seeking for the producers of rapeseed only that consideration to which they were entitled.
The production of rapeseed in the prairie provinces has developed largely because the farmers in that area have found that it is an acceptable alternative to the growing of wheat. With a substantial export market it has become a very important cash crop. In recent years Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, France and West Germany have provided the most important markets, although at least seven other countries have consistently imported this grain from Canada. As a result, exports of rapeseed have risen roughly from 60 million pounds in 1956 to a high of 284 million pounds in 1958, a further 222 million pounds in 1959 and to 259,625,000 pounds in 1960. I have some interesting comparisons in our export business of rapeseed. In 1958, the Netherlands took 123,154,000 pounds but in 1959 Italy led with 100,939,000 pounds. Over those years these two countries have been a very important market for this product.
It is also interesting to note that rapeseed production in pounds has risen from 13,900,000 pounds in 1953 to 551 million pounds. In my own province of Manitoba in the same period the production was as follows: In 1953 we produced 4,300,000 pounds; in 196061, 26 million pounds.
Wide variations in the acreage sown to this crop in the past can be attributed to the price received by the producer. The adjustment in the freight rate to that prevailing for flax, while adding only a fraction of a cent a pound, will help to provide a suitable cash crop with approximately the same amount of earnings as from a similar acreage sown to wheat. This incentive to switch from wheat should help reduce our surplus of that grain. It is another step forward in bringing our farm production in line with our market requirements and in our ability to adjust to changing conditions.
Wheat acreage has remained fairly constant in recent years although there was a sharp reduction amounting to some 3 million acres from the period 1948 to 1952. The reduction has been mostly in those areas that have been able to find suitable alternative crops. The reduction of wheat acreage, however, has been
Railway Act
more than paralleled by the increases in yield through better farming methods and improved types of seed. There is every reason to believe that the ultimate has not yet been reached in improved wheat yields. It is therefore going to be necessary to continue to encourage the production of other grains. Rapeseed is one of those grains that fit into this production picture exceedingly well.
This grain has a wide variety of uses and continued research in respect of this important product may well add further to its usefulness in the economy of the nation.
Just briefly, some of the uses are its importance in the making of margarine and cooking oil; its use as a marine engine lubricant. It is now being used experimentally as a component of lubricants for engines of cars and trucks.
The processing plants for this seed are located strategically in the production areas. In Manitoba the plant is at Altona. In Alberta it is at Lethbridge and in Saskatchewan at Saskatoon. I believe that the action of the government in introducing this bill and applying the Crowsnest rates to rapeseed should further reassure the farmers of western Canada, as mentioned by the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Horner), that those rates will continue to apply to western grains as long as this government remains in office.
If any further reassurance had been needed, this bill placing rapeseed on the same freight rate basis as flax is this government's answer to those critics who have been implying that changes in the Crowsnest rates were under consideration.
I should like to commend the government for taking action at this time, action that will assure the producers the new rates for the coming year, which should add considerably to the income the farmer may expect from that crop in the fall. At the same time I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale on the services he has rendered the western agricultural community. I am sure that not only will all farmers be pleased with his efforts but the farmers of his own riding, where such a large percentage of the rapeseed is grown, will be able to show their support for his action at the proper time.

AMENDMENT RESPECTING USE OF TRADING STAMPS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-34, to amend the Criminal Code (trading stamps).
He said: Mr. Speaker, this particular bill was before the house during last session for a rather lengthy debate. Perhaps it would not be well at this time to go into all the arguments pro and con in an attempt to reinforce or refute them. However, let me say

that some years ago the Criminal Code was amended to ban in effect the use and distribution of trading stamps. The Criminal Code now contains a definition of trading stamps, even though it is not in the same words as it was when originally enacted. The section contains a number of loopholes which allow the use of trading stamps in those provinces in which they are not banned by the provincial government, and allow trading stamps to be distributed even though the Criminal Code says this practice is illegal. The amending bill proposes to block these particular loopholes.
Since this matter was last debated in the house there have been a number of actions with regard to trading stamps, some in the courts and others by way of briefs presented to the government. A couple of well known and responsible organizations in this nation, notably the retail merchants association and the Canadian Association of Consumers, have made representations to the government calling for a ban on the use of trading stamps at the federal level. The government indicated tacit approval of the request made by these organizations, but as with so many other things, this government took no action but merely expressed sympathy. This bill before us provides an opportunity for something to be done and provides an opportunity for this government to do what it indicated it wanted to do.
The two organizations I have mentioned, as well as many others, consider that trading stamps are an insidious blight on our economy; that they tend to promote a monopoly and a concentration of power over the economy in the particular field in which trading stamps are used; that there is an air of dishonesty attached to them. These organizations feel that the use of stamps results in higher prices to the consumer. For these reasons, I think this house should give speedy passage to this bill, especially in view of the fact an extensive discussion took place on this subject last year.
